s10.meta.title: Proof of Life
s10.board.elena.title: Elena Christofi
s10.board.elena.sub: 38, paralegal, Bristol. Your client. It is her phone, her nine years, and she is sitting across the table while you read it.
s10.board.bobby.title: Bobby
s10.board.bobby.sub: Andreas Solomou. Anaesthetist, London. Engaged to her since 2022. Nine years of messages and not one photograph taken that day.
s10.board.andreas.title: The real Andreas Solomou
s10.board.andreas.sub: 41. Married, two children. A public profile he uses about twice a year, and every photograph on it has been sent to her. He has never heard of her.
s10.board.family.title: Forty of us in a house built for four
s10.board.family.sub: Name days, christenings, Thursday at Marianna's. Seven years of photographs, and everybody is in them.
s10.board.accounts.title: Thirty-nine accounts
s10.board.accounts.sub: A wife. A doctor. A brother. A hospital administrator. Two of them are in her contacts under their own names.
s10.board.money.sub: The total she ever sent. Three transfers in nine years. This was never about money.
s10.board.nia.title: Nia
s10.board.nia.sub: Her friend since 2016. Said it in 2018, in 2020, in 2023. Said it kindly every time.
s10.board.nadia.title: Nadia Solomou
s10.board.nadia.sub: His wife. Wrote to Elena in 2019 and again in 2024, both times to tell her what kind of woman she was. Elena has never seen her face and has never doubted her.

s10.client_chat.cc_001: I am going to say all of this at once and quickly, because if I stop I will not start again.
s10.client_chat.cc_002: My name is Elena Christofi. For nine years I was in a relationship with a man called Andreas Solomou, who everybody calls Bobby. We were engaged in 2022. I have never met him.
s10.client_chat.cc_003: I know how that sounds. I am a paralegal. I check documents for a living. I have sat in this chair for nine years being the most careful person in every room and I did not check the only thing that mattered.
s10.client_chat.cc_004: In March I found the real Andreas Solomou. He is married. He has two children. He lives close enough that I could have driven there any weekend of the last nine years, and he had never heard my name in his life. He was very kind about it, which was somehow the worst part of that day.
s10.client_chat.cc_005: So somebody has been writing to me since 2017. Not one person. Not a wife, a doctor, a brother, a hospital. I have counted thirty-nine accounts and I am not confident that is all of them.
s10.client_chat.cc_006: It is my phone. I am giving you my own phone. I am going to sit here while you read it. I have already read it, and I would rather not be alone with it.
s10.client_chat.cc_007: The police have told me there is probably no offence. My solicitor says there might be a civil claim. Before any of that I want to know who. Will you find out?
s10.client_chat.cc_008: Thank you. Start at the beginning and do not be careful with me. I have spent nine years being handled gently by somebody and look where it got me.
s10.client_chat.cc_009: One thing. Everything is still on there. I have not deleted a single message and I want you to know that was a decision, not an accident.
s10.interstitial.is1_001: Nine years and not one video call. You typed it and I actually laughed.
s10.interstitial.is1_002: There was always a reason. Bad line. On a ward. Night shift. Phone broken. Ex-wife tracking him. And every single reason was reasonable, that is the thing nobody understands about this.
s10.interstitial.is1_003: One a week for nine years is four hundred and sixty-eight reasons. I never once put them in a row. Keep going.
s10.interstitial.is2_002: Every account. Bobby, Nadia, the doctor, the brother, all of them, silent between seven and nine on a Thursday evening, for nine years.
s10.interstitial.is2_003: Thursday is my aunt Marianna's. It has been Thursday at Marianna's since before I was born. Forty of us, no phones at the table, she takes them off you at the door like a nightclub.
s10.interstitial.is2_004: I have been in that room for nine years. Do not tell me yet. Just keep going.
s10.interstitial.is3_001: I have looked at the photographs.
s10.interstitial.is3_002: Six photographs in the family album, going back to 2019. She is in four of them. That is not strange. She is my cousin. She is at everything.
s10.interstitial.is3_003: I am in all four of them too. Holding the baby. My arm around somebody. A plate on my knees. At the sink. My hands are full in every single one. Hers are not.
s10.interstitial.is3_004: She was eighteen when it started. I want you to finish it properly and I want you to be sure.
s10.closing_chat.cl_001: She admitted it on Tuesday. Not to me — to her mother, who rang me at half past eleven at night and could not get the sentence out.
s10.closing_chat.cl_002: Nine years, thirty-nine accounts, and she says it started as a joke. I have decided to believe that, because the alternative is that an eighteen-year-old sat down and planned this, and I would like to keep one thing.
s10.closing_chat.cl_003: Right. Wexley has laid out what I can do and none of it is what I want, which is for the last nine years not to have happened.
s10.closing_chat.cl_004: One. Civil claim. Harassment. It is the only thing that fits, because there is no offence in this country called pretending to be somebody for nine years. I would probably win. It would be a public judgment with both our names on it and every person we are related to would read it.
s10.closing_chat.cl_005: Two. Push the police anyway. Make them take a statement, make them open a file, make them write it down even if nothing is ever charged. It costs me nothing and buys me nothing except that it exists on a system somewhere.
s10.closing_chat.cl_006: Three, and this is the one I keep coming back to at four in the morning.
s10.closing_chat.cl_007: No court. Thursday, at Marianna's, all of them in the room, and I put it on the table myself and let the family decide what happens to her.
s10.closing_chat.cl_008: You should know what that costs before you answer. Half of them will not believe me. Some of them will believe me and decide it is kinder to everybody if it is never mentioned again. And her mother has hosted every Thursday of my life.
s10.closing_chat.cl_009: I have also thought about what it costs her, which I am aware is not my job any more.
s10.closing_chat.cl_010: She is twenty-seven and she has done nothing else with those nine years either. That is the part I cannot put down.
s10.closing_chat.cl_011: Tell me. You have read all of it now, which makes you the only person alive who has.
s10.closing_chat.cl_011.opt1: The civil claim. Make it a judgment.
s10.closing_chat.cl_011.opt2: The police file. Make it exist.
s10.closing_chat.cl_011.opt3: Thursday. Put it on the table.
s10.closing_chat.cl_013: The claim, then. Wexley will be pleased, she has been waiting for me to say it for a fortnight.
s10.closing_chat.cl_014: I want it written down somewhere that I did not do this to be paid. I did it so a judge would put in writing that it happened. For nine years, the only person who could confirm anything about my life was her.
s10.closing_chat.cl_015: The file, then. A statement, a crime number, and almost certainly nothing after that.
s10.closing_chat.cl_016: Nia asked me why I would bother. I said: in thirty years, somebody is going to do this to somebody else. There should be more than nothing in the drawer. She said that was the most paralegal sentence she had ever heard.
s10.closing_chat.cl_018: If I take it to a court I hand it to strangers and I get an outcome. If I take it to that room I hand it to the only people who were actually there, and I get whatever they are. I have decided I would rather be in the room.
s10.closing_chat.cl_019: Thank you. Genuinely. You are the first person in nine years who looked at all of it and did not once ask me how I could have been so stupid.
s10.ending.civil:
The claim was issued in September. It settled eleven months later, four days before trial, for a sum neither side is allowed to state. Elena has described it in writing as 'less than the legal costs and more than I expected'.

The settlement carries an admission and a letter of apology. The letter runs to two pages. Elena has read it once.

Because it settled, there is no judgment, which is the thing she actually wanted. Her solicitor had warned her this was the likeliest outcome and she pressed on anyway, and says she would again.

Sophia Christofi was dismissed from the pharmacy in the November after the firm's insurers made enquiries. She lives in Swindon now. Marianna still hosts Thursday. Elena has not been since the claim was issued, and Marianna has telephoned her every single Thursday at half past eight, for eleven months, and left the same message, which is: the plate is out.

The real Andreas Solomou gave a two-paragraph witness statement confirming he does not know Elena Christofi and never has. He asked, through his solicitor, whether she was all right. Nobody had asked her that in a legal document before and she says it undid her more than the settlement did.
s10.ending.police:
Avon and Somerset took a statement over two visits totalling nine hours. The crime number exists. Nothing was ever charged.

The file records the offence as harassment, considered under section 2. It gives the reason for no further action as evidential: nine years of contact that the complainant, on the face of the record, welcomed and returned. She was not tricked into contacting these accounts. She chose to reply to them. Elena has read that sentence perhaps forty times and has stopped arguing with it.

What the file does is exist. In the third year an officer from another force rang her about a case with the same shape in Swansea — thirty-plus accounts, one operator, six years — because a search had surfaced her statement. She spoke to that woman for two hours. That call is the only outcome of this route and Elena considers it sufficient.

Sophia was interviewed under caution once and answered every question. Nothing followed. She is still in Bristol, still at the pharmacy, and still at Thursday. Elena is not.

The last message Elena sent was: I did the boring one. Somebody has to be in the drawer.
s10.ending.family:
She did it on the fourth Thursday in June, in her aunt's front room, with thirty-one people in it and the food already on the table.

What happened is not fully recorded because Elena has only ever described it once. Her father stood up first. Her aunt Marianna did not speak for eleven minutes and then asked Sophia one question, in Greek, which Elena has not translated for anybody. Sophia answered it. Four people left before the answer.

There was no court, no claim, no crime number. Nothing at all in writing. Until Elena sat down two days later and typed it herself, for herself, and saved it in the folder with everything else.

The family split roughly as she predicted, though not along the lines she predicted. Two people she had counted on told her to let it go for her aunt's sake. Three she had barely spoken to in a decade rang her that week and have rung her since. Her father has not spoken to his sister since June and has begun to.

Sophia is in a supervised programme through her GP and writes to Elena about once a month. Elena does not reply and does not delete them, which she says is exactly what she did for nine years and she is aware of that and is doing it anyway.

Marianna hosts Thursday. Elena goes. They have never discussed it again and both of them know the other one is not going to be the first to.

El, you asked me to send this. I have been sitting on it for two days. I didn't want to be the one.

It's Costas and Eleni's wedding. My cousin was there. She tagged about ninety people and one of them is a consultant anaesthetist from Cardiff called Andreas Solomou, and El, it's him. It's the face. It's the same face as every photograph you have ever shown me.

s10.mail.gm_004.subject: Harassment — preliminary advice
s10.mail.gm_004.body:
Elena,

As promised, the short version in writing.

There is no criminal offence in England and Wales of impersonating a person online in order to conduct a relationship. Fraud requires a gain or a loss and £312 over nine years will not carry it. Malicious communications requires the messages to be grossly offensive, or false with intent to cause distress. That could be argued. But the messages you received were, on their face, affectionate.

What fits is harassment: a course of conduct, over a period, causing alarm or distress, which the perpetrator knew or ought to have known amounted to harassment. Both criminal (s.2) and civil (s.3) routes exist. The civil route does not require the police or the CPS to be interested, which on the facts is likely to be the deciding factor.

I want to be straight with you about the cost of the civil route, and I do not mean the fees. It will be public, it will carry both names, and every member of your family will read it.

Come in Thursday. Bring the chronology.

Hannah Wexley
s10.mail.gm_005.subject: (no subject)
s10.mail.gm_005.body:
I have started this eleven times.

I am not going to explain it. There is no explanation that is not an excuse. I have read enough of my own excuses for one lifetime.

It started as a joke. I was eighteen and you were sad about Michalis and I made an account for about a week to make you laugh and then you were happy and I did not know how to stop being the reason.

Every year it got harder to stop and easier to keep going and I know exactly how that sounds.

I am not asking you for anything. I am telling you because Mum asked me a question on Tuesday and I could not lie to her face, which I want you to notice, because I could always lie to yours.

S.

s10.notes.note_001.title: Reasons
s10.notes.note_001.block_001: I started this in 2021 to prove to Nia that there was always a reason, and then I kept it, which tells you something.
s10.notes.note_001.block_002: bad line · on a ward · night shift · phone in a locker · front camera cracked · the trust blocks video apps · ex-wife has access to his cloud · doesn't want me to see him this thin
s10.notes.note_001.block_003: doesn't want the first time to be through a screen · doesn't photograph well · superstitious about it · says he'll do it when he's well
s10.notes.note_001.block_004: Every one of these is a real reason. I know men who would say any of them.
s10.notes.note_001.block_005: One a week for nine years is four hundred and sixty-eight of them and I have never once put them in a row until today.
s10.notes.note_002.title: Thursdays
s10.notes.note_002.block_001: Marianna's, 7 till late, since before I was born. Phones in the bowl at the door, she is militant about it.
s10.notes.note_002.block_002: Bobby has never messaged me on a Thursday evening. Not once in nine years. I used to think it was because he knew it was family night and was being respectful.
s10.notes.note_002.block_003: Nadia has never messaged me on a Thursday evening.
s10.notes.note_002.block_004: Dr Ferris has never messaged me on a Thursday evening.
s10.notes.note_002.block_005: His brother. The hospital administrator. The man from the insurance. None of them. Not one of the thirty-nine, in nine years, between seven and nine on a Thursday.
s10.notes.note_002.block_006: (Everything I have screenshotted since March is in the album called everything, and the note in the other folder. Both 0911. I did not have to look that up, which is its own small piece of evidence about me.)
s10.notes.note_003.block_001: Written at four in the morning on the twentieth of March, which I am putting at the top so that later I know I was not calm.
s10.notes.note_003.block_002: I am writing this down because in about a year, I am going to want to know exactly what I thought on the day I found out. I do not trust myself to remember it kindly.
s10.notes.note_003.block_003: What I feel is not grief for him. He was never there, so there is nothing to grieve. What I feel is that somebody watched me for nine years the way you watch a programme.
s10.notes.note_003.block_004: And that they were in the room for a lot of it. Sitting on the arm of the sofa. Asking me how he was.
s10.notes.note_003.block_005: I have not written the name yet. I will when I am sure. Being sure is the only thing I have left that is mine.

s10.memos.vm_001.title: 9 Nov
s10.memos.vm_001.transcript: It's me. I know it's late. I'm not going to keep you. I just wanted to say the thing I couldn't say on the phone with people around. Today is nine years since the people-you-may-know message. I have counted every one of them. Right. Go to sleep. I'll ring you tomorrow at the usual.
s10.memos.vm_002.transcript: It is quarter to four in the morning on the twentieth of March. I am recording this because I want to know later what my own voice sounded like tonight. [pause] I am fine. That is the strange part. I keep waiting to fall apart about a man and it is not happening, because there was no man. What I keep getting instead is small things. I told her about the miscarriage before I told my mother. She was in the kitchen when I did it. She made me tea and then she went home and wrote to me as him about it. [pause] I have not said that out loud before and I am not going to again.
s10.lock.step_001.hint: Her own note gives the album code outright: the day he first messaged her, day and month, four digits.
s10.question.q01.title: Nine years
s10.question.q01.question: Across nine years and thousands of hours of contact, there is one ordinary thing that never once happened between them. What?
s10.question.q02.title: Seventy kilometres
s10.question.q02.question: Every photograph she was sent belongs to a real man with an ordinary public profile. Where does he actually live?
s10.question.q03.title: The call log
s10.question.q03.question: There are thousands of calls from that number over nine years. One thing is true of every one of them. What?
s10.question.q03.opt3: They were all from the same mast
s10.question.q04.title: Four months
s10.question.q04.question: In 2019 he vanished for four months and came back with an explanation that she accepted. What was he supposedly in?
s10.question.q05.title: One week in March 2021
s10.question.q05.question: Four accounts told her four things in the same week. Three of them can be true at once. Tap the one that cannot.
s10.question.q05.sn0: Bobby: 'On the ward till Friday, they've moved me to the cardiac unit, no phones past the doors.'
s10.question.q05.sn1: Dr Ferris: 'He's stable. He has asked that you don't come to the hospital and I'd normally push back on that.'
s10.question.q05.sn2: Nadia: 'He rang me from the car this afternoon. He sounded terrible. Whatever you said to him, don't.'
s10.question.q05.sn3: Bobby's brother: 'Family only on the unit, I'm sorry. I'll tell him you asked.'
s10.question.q06.title: His wife
s10.question.q06.question: For three years a woman messaged her — first furious, then apologetic, finally almost kind. She is one of the thirty-nine. What is her name?
s10.question.q07.title: Two hours a week
s10.question.q07.question: Every one of the thirty-nine accounts goes completely silent in the same two-hour window every week, for nine years, without a single exception. Which day?
s10.question.q08.title: One thing, no explanation
s10.question.q08.question: In 2023 she asked him to send a photograph of himself that could not be an old one. What did she ask him to hold up in it?
s10.question.q09.title: 14 March
s10.question.q09.question: She was told he was in a London hospital that day. The real man was somewhere else, photographed and tagged. Where?
s10.question.q10.title: Three hundred and twelve pounds
s10.question.q10.question: She sent money three times in nine years, £312 in total. What was the largest of the three for?
s10.question.q11.title: The tell
s10.question.q11.question: One word appears in all thirty-nine accounts, wrong the same way every time. Thirty-nine people could not share that. What kind of mistake is it?
s10.question.q12.title: Four streets away
s10.question.q12.question: Thirty-nine accounts, one connection, one postcode. One person was there every Thursday and in most of the family photographs. Who?
s10.question.q13.title: Look again
s10.question.q13.question: Open the Family album and read the four photographs she is in, from 2019 to 2025. In every one of them her hands are doing the same thing. What is she holding?
s10.question.q14.title: The eleventh attempt
s10.question.q14.question: Her explanation came at last, and refused to be one. She names what it was at the start, before it became nine years. What?
s10.question.q15.title: What it is called
s10.question.q15.question: Being somebody else for nine years is not an offence here. Her solicitor found the one thing that fits. What is it?

s10.mail.f_gm_101.body:
Dear Elena,

As discussed, this letter sets out the basis on which we are instructed.

We are instructed on a civil claim under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. We are not instructed in relation to any criminal complaint. I have explained why and you told me you had already worked it out yourself, which I do not doubt.

Our charging rate is £280 per hour. I have capped the first stage at £1,500 and I will tell you before we go past it.

Hannah Wexley

Marianna,

I am not coming Thursday and I want to explain why in a way that does not make you choose.

It is not that I cannot look at her. I can look at her, I did it for nine years without knowing and I could probably do it now.

It is the bowl by the door. I cannot walk past that bowl and put my phone in it and sit down, knowing what those two hours were for, and eat your lamb, and be
s10.notes.f_note_101.title: Things I have told him
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_001: Started this because Nia said I don't talk to anybody. Proof that I do.
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_002: Mum. All of it, including the last week, which I have never said out loud to anyone including Dad.
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_003: The miscarriage. Told him on the Tuesday. Told Nia on the Friday. Told nobody in the family, ever.
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_004: What I actually think of Marchbank.
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_005: The thing I did at nineteen. He is the only person alive who knows about that.
s10.notes.f_note_101.block_006: Eight things. Eight things nobody else has and he has all eight.
s10.notes.f_note_102.title: Ring times
s10.notes.f_note_102.block_001: He rings. I don't ring — the number never connects, it's a work handset and it's locked down.
s10.notes.f_note_102.block_002: Tuesdays and Fridays about nine. Sometimes Sunday. Never Thursday, he knows it's family.
s10.notes.f_note_102.block_003: Longest was 3 hours 50, the night after Mum's anniversary.
s10.notes.f_note_102.block_004: I have tried his number twice in nine years. Once in 2025 and once in January. Both times nothing, and both times he rang me within ten minutes and was lovely about it.
s10.notes.f_note_102.block_005: Writing that down has made it look like something. It is not something. It is a locked-down work handset.
s10.notes.f_note_103.title: What I have to do
s10.notes.f_note_103.block_002: Report the accounts — sent 25/3. Expect nothing.
s10.notes.f_note_103.block_004: Tell Dad. Not Marianna. Dad first, on his own, in his kitchen.
s10.notes.f_note_103.block_005: Decide about Thursday. Not this week. Not next week either.
s10.notes.f_note_111.block_001: Four in the morning, five days in. Making a list of what is actually gone, because I keep saying "everything" and everything is not a thing.
s10.notes.f_note_111.block_002: Gone: the person I talked to at night for nine years. That one is real and I am allowed it.
s10.notes.f_note_111.block_003: Gone: nine years of Thursdays. Not the future ones. The ones I already had, which were fine at the time and are not fine now.
s10.notes.f_note_111.block_004: Gone: knowing what my own face looked like to her. She watched me being happy about something she was typing. She must have had a face on while she did it. I will never know what it was.
s10.notes.f_note_111.block_005: Not gone: Dad. Nia. The job. The flat. Me. Writing that down because at four in the morning the list looks shorter than it is.
s10.notes.f_note_112.block_001: Wexley says a claim is a public document and her name goes in it.
s10.notes.f_note_112.block_002: She is twenty-seven. She has a job she got by herself. She was proud of it, in a way I remember, because I was there. I was pleased. I sent her a message with three exclamation marks.
s10.notes.f_note_112.block_003: I have written out both versions of the rest of my life. In one of them I do it. In the other I don't. In neither of them do I get the nine years back. I did not expect that to be the deciding factor, and it is not. But I keep writing it down.
s10.notes.f_note_112.block_004: What Hannah actually said: not bringing one is a decision you are allowed to make.
s10.notes.f_note_112.block_005: Nobody has said that to me about anything in nine years. Everything has always been a thing I had to be patient about.

s10.photos.ph_020.document:
Photograph of a christening party in a church hall. Twenty-odd people, paper cups, a trestle table with a cake on it.

  Elena is holding the baby and looking at whoever is taking the picture. At the edge of the group, half turned away from the camera, Sophia is standing with a phone held low against her hip, screen up, thumb resting on it.
s10.photos.ph_021.document:
Photograph of a family lunch, taken down the length of the table.

  Nine people. Elena is halfway down on the left with her arm around the woman beside her. Across the table from her Sophia has one hand flat on a phone lying face up next to her plate, the way somebody keeps a hand on a glass.
s10.photos.ph_022.document:
Photograph of a garden in strong afternoon light.

  Two children on the grass and a dog. Elena is on the step with a plate on her knees. Sophia is in the garden chair behind her with a phone in her lap and her thumb on the screen, not looking at the children.
s10.photos.ph_023.document:
Photograph of a kitchen on Christmas Eve, taken late, most of the light coming from the hood over the cooker.

  Elena is at the sink with her sleeves pushed up. Sophia is standing against the counter behind her with a phone in her left hand, held up and angled away, her face lit by it.
s10.photos.ph_034.document:
Photograph of a wooden bowl on a hall table with four phones in it, taken from above.

  A house rule, evidently: phones go in the bowl. Four of them, and the family in that evening's other photographs is five.
